title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production as Elon Musk focuses on robotics and AI
content:
Elon Musk has announced that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck, marking the end of a failed effort to take a chunk of the lucrative market for pickups in the US.
The billionaire chief executive said production of the car would stop in about the middle of next year at the company’s factory in Texas in order to use the plant for the Cybercab, its self-driving taxi.
Musk did not say whether Tesla had plans to produce the vehicle in another factory, although that would probably require significant investment for the specialised tooling needed to make it.
Musk has pinned hopes for Tesla on robotics, artificial intelligence and an autonomous driving fleet rather than following the traditional carmakers’ approach of developing a steady stream of new models to entice private buyers.
It caps a tricky week for the world’s richest person, after Republican candidates he had backed with $446m (£332m) in donations lost in the US midterm elections. The paper value of Musk’s fortune fell by $113bn after the extent of the rout became clear, as stock market investors questioned whether a Democrat-led Congress could slow the pace of the AI boom.
Tesla shares fell by 11% on Thursday, while his AI and rocket launch company, SpaceX, dropped by 9%.
Tesla started deliveries of the Cybertruck in late 2023, after several long delays as the company tried to cope with the technical challenges of producing such an unusual vehicle – and particularly its steel shell.
The Cybertruck never made it on sale in Europe because it did not reach the required safety standards.
Even before sales began, Musk acknowledged how difficult it would be to make it a success. In a 2023 earnings call, he said: “We dug our own grave with Cybertruck,” and noted “enormous challenges” in increasing production and earning money from it.
Musk had said the company aimed to sell 200,000 Cybertrucks each year but it never approached that target. Tesla does not report sales of the trucks separately but in the third quarter of 2026 it delivered only 8,300 “other models”, which include the Cybertruck. The vast majority of its sales were the Model 3 saloon and the Model Y SUV, with 478,000 combined deliveries during the quarter.
Tesla also this year stopped production of its Model S and Model X, its premium saloon and SUV, amid declining sales for ageing products.
Tesla’s automotive focus has shifted to the Cybercab. Tesla has started offering paid trips in the car, which has space for two passengers and no steering wheel, in limited parts of Austin, Texas. However, it is unclear how quickly the company will be able to roll out the taxi service around the US or further afield amid close regulatory scrutiny of driverless car technology.
As well as the Cybercab, Tesla is still ramping up production of its long-delayed Semi electric lorry. Musk is also aiming to produce one other new model: the Roadster sportscar, which Musk revealed with a demonstration of a “flying car” version that used thrusters developed by SpaceX to drive up a curved ramp before flipping and landing. Tesla is aiming to start production of a road-bound version in 2028. Analysts do not expect the Roadster to make a large difference to Tesla’s future profits.
Beyond vehicles, the Texas factory will also be used to build Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robot.
Musk posted on X, the social network he owns: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

report.summary: Tesla will stop building the Cybertruck at its Texas plant around mid-2027, converting the line to Cybercab robotaxi and Optimus robot production as Musk pivots from pickups to AI and robotics.
report.background: The Cybertruck was Musk's bet on the profitable US full-size pickup market, where Ford, GM and Stellantis earn much of their profit. Tesla began deliveries in late 2023 after repeated delays caused by the stainless-steel exoskeleton's manufacturing difficulty, and the truck never passed European safety standards. Musk set a 200,000-per-year target but volumes stayed in the low thousands; Tesla reported just 8,300 combined deliveries of "other models" in Q3 2026. Meanwhile the company has discontinued the Model S and Model X, and its growth now rests on the Model 3/Y, the Semi lorry, the Cybercab robotaxi, the Optimus humanoid robot and a delayed Roadster. The shift comes amid investor anxiety about AI valuations after US midterm elections saw Musk-backed candidates lose.
key_points: Production ends mid-next year at Gigafactory Texas: Musk said the Cybertruck line will wind down around the middle of next year so the space can be used for higher-volume Cybercab output. He gave no indication the truck will be built elsewhere, which would require costly new tooling.

It missed its targets by an order of magnitude: Tesla aimed for 200,000 Cybertrucks a year but never came close. Q3 2026 saw only 8,300 deliveries across all "other models" including the truck, versus 478,000 combined Model 3 and Model Y sales.

The vehicle was engineering-heavy and geographically limited: the unusual stainless-steel body caused repeated delays, Musk admitted "we dug our own grave with Cybertruck", and it never met European safety standards so was never sold there.

Tesla's car business is narrowing while AI bets expand: Model S and Model X are already discontinued, the Cybercab is running paid driverless trips in parts of Austin, and Optimus robots will also be built at the Texas site.

It caps a rough week for Musk: after Republican candidates he funded with $446m lost the midterms, Tesla shares fell 11% and SpaceX 9%, cutting $113bn from his paper fortune as investors questioned AI spending under a Democrat-led Congress.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a signal that Tesla is repositioning from carmaker to embodied-AI company: capital and factory floor space are moving from low-volume metal-bending to robotaxi fleets and humanoid robots. That raises the stakes in the robotaxi race against Waymo and Chinese operators, and adds a well-funded contender to the humanoid-robot field currently led by Figure, Agility and Chinese startups. For developers, it means more real-world data from driverless deployments and a likely expansion of Tesla's robotaxi and Optimus software stacks. For regular users, the practical effect is minimal today: Cybertruck owners keep their trucks but face weaker resale values and long-term parts support questions, while everyday drivers are more likely to encounter a driverless Tesla taxi than a new Cybertruck.
report.tools: To follow the underlying technology, watch Tesla's FSD and Cybercab rollout in Austin, plus Optimus progress. Open-source equivalents worth trying: ROS 2 for robotics middleware, NVIDIA Isaac Sim and MuJoCo for simulation, Hugging Face's LeRobot for low-cost robot learning, and comma.ai's openpilot for driver-assistance research. Waymo's safety reports and California DMV robotaxi filings are useful benchmarks for regulatory comparison.
